Executor note: the card itself suggests `@object-ui/app-shell` (1259 specifiers) may deserve a split — the dispatching seat may take the six small packages first and file app-shell separately rather than one oversized PR; either way delete the ledger entries in the same commit per the ratchet.

Size/model suggestion: M, `mode:subagent`.

## Scope: six packages now, `app-shell` separately — pre-authorised

The card says `@object-ui/app-shell` at **1259 specifiers** "probably deserves its own card", and the triage seat authorised the split explicitly:

> the dispatching seat may take the six small packages first and file `app-shell` separately rather than one oversized PR; **either way delete the ledger entries in the same commit per the ratchet.**

So: **the six**, and I am filing `app-shell` as its own card. ⛔ Do not touch `packages/app-shell` here.

The six are where the leverage is, and it is not proportional to their size: the **11 packages that "fail on somebody else's file"** all die on `mobile/dist/useBreakpoint`, `permissions/dist/PermissionProvider` or `providers/dist/DataSourceProvider` — **all three inside your six.** `mobile` (27) and `permissions` (14) are the two cheapest entries in the whole table and unblock six and four downstream packages respectively. **Measure the before/after loadable count and put it in the PR body** — the card predicts 17 → 35 of 39 for all seven; with `app-shell` deferred your number will differ, and I want yours, not the card's.

## The fix shape, already proven on four packages in #4538

1. **Append the explicit extension to every relative specifier the build emits** — `./x` → `./x.js`, a directory import → `./x/index.js`. ⚠️ **Resolve each one against the filesystem rather than pattern-matching**: a specifier inside a comment must be left alone, and `./x` may be a file or a directory. A regex sweep over 414 specifiers is how this card comes back.
2. Optionally pin `module`/`moduleResolution` to `nodenext` in **that package's own** `tsconfig.json`, which turns a missing extension into a compile error (TS2835/TS2834) instead of a review item — done for `packages/react` in #4538. ⛔ **Never the root `tsconfig.json`**: 38 packages extend it and a repo-wide flip is a different, much larger change.
3. **Delete each cleared package's entry from `SPECIFIER_DEBT` in `scripts/check-node-esm-load.mjs` in the same commit.** The ledger is a ratchet and **fails on a stale entry**, so a cleared package with its entry left behind turns CI red — which is the ledger working.

## Why this matters, stated so the verification aims at it

Node's ESM resolver does **not** extension-search relative specifiers, and a bare `tsc` never rewrites them — so an extensionless `./Foo` in source is an extensionless `./Foo` in the published `dist`, and importing the entry under plain Node fails with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. **Bundled consumers are unaffected, which is exactly why everything is green today.** The gate that sees it is `pnpm check:node-esm-load`, not the test suite.

## Tests / verification

- `pnpm check:esm-specifiers` → **zero** for each of the six.
- `pnpm check:node-esm-load` → each of the six imports and evaluates, **and** report which of the 11 downstream packages became loadable as a result. That second number is the card's real payload.
- The packages' own suites stay green, run **from the repo root**.
- ⛔ Do not silence a failure by adding a ledger entry. The ledger only shrinks here.

Reverse-verify: revert one package's specifiers (pick `permissions` — 14, and four downstream packages depend on it), keep everything else, **predict what `check:node-esm-load` reports before running**, then run it. State per leg whether a build artifact sits between the edit and the thing under test — **for this card one certainly does**: the gate reads `dist`, so say how you rebuilt and how you know the artifact under test is the one you edited.

## Gates

Derive from your diff (`scripts/pm/dispatch-gates.mjs` is **objectstack-only**). Run vitest **from the repo root** — the reason is not that package-scoped runs are refused (17 packages own a standalone `vitest.config.ts` and are not refused) but that a package-scoped run uses **a different config than CI does**. Changeset per `check-changeset-presence.mjs`'s verdict — six released packages change, so expect one; `patch` or `minor`, ⛔ **never `major`**.

⛔ Do not background a long check and end your turn. ⛔ No exhaustive paginated API sweeps.

## Deliver

Draft PR against `main`, first body line **`Part of #5214`** — ⛔ not `Fixes`, because `app-shell` remains and this card must not close on merge. Push the branch early. Return the JSON report and post it as a comment whose first line is the literal `<!-- os-dev-report -->` marker.

#5357 is `pm:blocked` behind this card. The reason is a hot file, not the package boundary: both PRs delete entries from the same `SPECIFIER_DEBT` array in `scripts/check-node-esm-load.mjs`, so they cannot run in parallel. Its file surface is to be re-verified on the merged ref once this lands.

One correction to the arithmetic in the body above, for whoever reads these two cards together. The body says clearing all seven takes the load leg from 17 to 35 of 39. Split across the two cards that is **17 → 34** for the six here (six own-file entries plus the eleven that die on `mobile`, `permissions` or `providers` — all three inside the six), and **34 → 35** for `app-shell` alone, which unblocks only itself. The six carry essentially all of the leverage; `app-shell` is the largest package and the smallest incremental unlock. Both cards ask the dev for their own measured before/after rather than these numbers.

## Measured payload

The `+17` is the six packages plus **all 11 downstream packages that were failing on somebody else's file** — every one of them died on `mobile`, `permissions` or `providers`, all inside the six. 412 relative specifiers across 94 files, each resolved against the filesystem, then verified mechanically: 412 changed line pairs, **0** that were not a pure extension append, histogram `{'.js': 412}`. ## Two corrections this card's model needed — both from the dev, both worth keeping

**1. `fields` was never failing on its own file.** Its `dist` carries **0** extensionless specifiers even unfixed: its `tsc` step inherits the root's `noEmit: true` and only type-checks, while `dist` comes from vite, which resolves the specifiers away. The before-run attributes it `@object-ui/fields (via @object-ui/providers)`. So this card's "the 7 above, each failing on its own file" is **wrong for `fields`** — what made it loadable was fixing `providers`. Its source specifiers were real ratchet debt, not a live `dist` defect. Gate quirk behind the confusion filed as **#5367**.

**2. The "11 that fail on somebody else's file" table is a first-failure snapshot, not a dependency map.** The reverse-verification is what exposed it: reverting `permissions` alone predicted 5 entries red, **observed 10**. `plugin-calendar`, `plugin-designer`, `plugin-grid`, `plugin-list` and `plugin-view` depend on **both** `mobile` and `permissions`; the census recorded only whichever module each package hit first, so fixing `mobile` merely surfaced the second dependency. `plugin-timeline` did not flip, so it really is `mobile`-only. Anyone reading that table as a dependency graph will mispredict.

Both corrections are carried into #5357's body.

## Filed, not fixed

- **#5365** — `@object-ui/components` ships `dist/index.d.ts` with 21 extensionless relative re-exports, so any consumer pinning `nodenext`/`node16` sees every named export as missing (TS2305). Same defect class, different artifact, **no gate covers it**. This is what blocked the `nodenext` pin on `packages/fields`, and it will likely block it on `app-shell` too.
- **#5367** — `check-node-esm-load.mjs`'s `readTsconfig()` strips comments with regexes that are not string-aware, so the `/*` inside `"@/*"` destroys the JSON and the verdict comes from a catch block rather than the config. Currently fails **safe** (a parse failure grades as emitting, which widens the scan), so nothing is red today — but the documented safety margin is spent and invisible.

## Closing — all seven packages are done; this card was a phantom in the queue

Caught by the mandatory decision re-read while selecting round R11. This card was sitting in `pm:queue` + `domain:devx` and would have been dispatched to a dev; **every package it names has already been cleared.**

### The evidence

| scope | carrier | state |
|---|---|---|
| the six small packages (`fields`, `auth`, `mobile`, `collaboration`, `permissions`, `providers`) | PR #5369 | **merged** as `5458414a7` |
| `@object-ui/app-shell` (the seventh) | #5357 → PR #5383 | **merged**, #5357 closed 2026-08-20 |

And the ratchet agrees, read on current `origin/main`:

```
scripts/check-node-esm-load.mjs:314
export const SPECIFIER_DEBT = new Map();
```

**Empty.** The map that carried all seven entries has none left. The prior seat left this card open with a precise condition — *"the surviving `SPECIFIER_DEBT` entry on `main` still reads `objectui#5214` … while that string is on `main`, this issue number is still load-bearing"* — and #5383 deleted exactly that line. The condition is discharged, so the card is done.

### How it got here

The seat that landed PR #5369 deliberately left this open and **unlabelled**, explicitly deferring the close/keep-open call to triage:

> Whether this closes now (six of seven done, the seventh carrying its own card) or stays open as the tracking parent until #5357 lands is a call for the triage seat — the naked state is so the sweep picks it up rather than so it disappears.

The sweep did pick it up — but as a **first-touch grading** on 2026-08-23, which stamped `pm:queue` + `domain:devx` on the reading that *"the population is enumerated, the analysis is already done on #4538, and the ledger means the debt cannot grow while this waits."* That reasoning is about the card's original scope; it did not account for #5357 having landed three days earlier. A deliberately-naked tracking parent and an untriaged card are indistinguishable to a label-only sweep, which is exactly the failure mode the naked state was accepted to risk.

Closing as **completed**, keeping `domain:devx` so the lane's history stays readable.

### Still open, and genuinely so — the two findings this work produced

Neither is closed by this, and both are worth a reader's attention because they are the same defect class in artifacts no gate covers:

- **#5365** — `@object-ui/components` ships `dist/index.d.ts` with 21 extensionless relative re-exports, so any consumer pinning `nodenext`/`node16` sees every named export as missing (TS2305). This is what blocked the `nodenext` pin on `packages/fields`. `check:esm-specifiers` correctly scopes itself to specifier-preserving `.js` builds and `check:node-esm-load` only `import()`s the runtime entry, so **nothing sees it**.
- **#5367** — `check-node-esm-load.mjs`'s `readTsconfig()` strips comments with regexes that are not string-aware, so the `/*` inside `"@/*"` destroys the JSON and `effectiveNoEmit()` answers from its catch block rather than from the config. Currently fails **safe**, but the documented safety margin is spent and invisible.

Also worth preserving from this card's history, since both corrections outlive it:

1. **`fields` was never failing on its own file** — its `dist` carries zero extensionless specifiers even unfixed (its `tsc` inherits the root's `noEmit: true`; `dist` comes from vite). Fixing `providers` is what made it loadable.
2. **The "11 that fail on somebody else's file" table is a first-failure snapshot, not a dependency map.** PR #5369's reverse-verification predicted 5 red and observed **10**, because five packages depend on both `mobile` and `permissions` and the census recorded only whichever each hit first. Anyone reading that table as a dependency graph will mispredict.

Final measured payload across both cards: **17 → 35 of 39** published ESM entries import and evaluate under plain Node. The remaining four are ledgered and explained (`plugin-dashboard` + `plugin-map` on third-party `.css`; `create-plugin` + `runner` not importable by design).
